questions.question: State the two universal rules about bond breaking and bond forming, define the heat of reaction ΔH with its units, and explain why a reaction that warms its surroundings nevertheless has a negative ΔH.
questions.expected_answer: Breaking a chemical bond always absorbs energy, because attracted particles must be forced apart; forming a chemical bond always releases energy. The heat of reaction ΔH is the potential energy of the products minus the potential energy of the reactants — ΔH = E(products) − E(reactants) — in kilojoules or kilojoules per mole. In an exothermic reaction the bond-forming payout exceeds the bond-breaking cost, so the surplus is exported to the surroundings as heat and the products finish at lower potential energy than the reactants. ΔH describes the system — the chemicals — not the surroundings: the chemicals end with less stored energy, so the subtraction is negative, even though the surroundings receive that energy and warm up. Pinning the sign to the warm beaker instead of the chemicals is the classic inversion error.

questions.question: Define activation energy and the activated complex, and use both to explain why propane in a gas heater only burns after the igniter sparks, yet the flame then keeps itself alight.
questions.expected_answer: Activation energy is the minimum energy colliding particles need in order to react — on the graph, the climb from the reactants' level to the summit. The activated complex is the unstable transition state of maximum potential energy at that summit, with old bonds partly broken and new bonds partly formed; it lasts only for the instant of a collision, then falls forward into products or back into reactants. At room temperature almost no propane-oxygen collisions carry enough energy to cover this admission price, so the gas flows past unburnt even though combustion is strongly exothermic. The spark supplies the activation energy for a small number of molecules; their reaction releases far more energy than the spark invested, and that surplus supplies the activation energy for neighbouring molecules. The combustion therefore funds its own continuation, which is why one spark keeps the flame burning.

questions.question: A potential energy graph shows reactants at 80 kJ, a summit at 170 kJ and products at 30 kJ. Calculate the forward activation energy, the forward ΔH, and the reverse activation energy. Then state precisely what a catalyst changes on this graph and what it leaves untouched.
questions.expected_answer: Forward activation energy: 170 − 80 = 90 kJ. Forward ΔH: 30 − 80 = −50 kJ, so the reaction is exothermic. Reverse activation energy: 170 − 30 = 140 kJ, with reverse ΔH = +50 kJ. Self-check: the two activation energies differ by exactly the magnitude of ΔH (140 − 90 = 50). A catalyst provides an alternative pathway of lower activation energy, so only the summit drops — for example from 170 kJ to 130 kJ, cutting the forward climb from 90 kJ to 50 kJ and the reverse climb from 140 kJ to 100 kJ. The reactant and product levels do not move, so ΔH is completely unchanged: the reaction becomes faster but releases exactly the same total energy, and the catalyst is recovered chemically unchanged.
